summary:
Marstronaut is an interactive 3D explorer of Mars with real terrain, NASA imagery and walking-route planning.

You can fly around a detailed 3D model of the planet, jump between landmarks like Jezero Crater, Gale Crater and Olympus Mons, and plan a route across the surface. Pick two or more places and the app finds a path between them, draws it on the terrain and tells you how long the trip would take an astronaut on foot.

The globe is built with CesiumJS and a Mars 3D terrain tileset streamed from Cesium ion. It has custom drag-to-rotate and scroll zoom, and the camera can’t go underground. You can switch between a 3D globe and a flat 2D map, and between three map layers: the 3D surface, MOLA color-shaded elevation and the Viking color mosaic, both from NASA Mars Trek.

There are 15 landmarks. The interface has a hand-drawn crayon look, with an onboarding dialogue, sound effects and an achievement popup, all of which can be skipped.

Route planning works like this. You add stops from the landmark list or type your own latitude and longitude. For every pair of consecutive stops, the app asks a pathfinding backend for a route. The backend scores the terrain by slope, surface type, temperature and points of interest. The frontend then joins the legs into one route and shows the total distance, walking time, EVA sols, maximum slope and total ascent and descent.
details:
What it does and how it works: Marstronaut is a web app that lets anyone explore Mars in 3D and plan a walking route across its surface. You fly around a detailed model of the planet, jump to landmarks like Jezero Crater, Gale Crater and Olympus Mons, and read short story-style facts about each one. You can also pick two or more places, and the app finds a path between them, draws it on the terrain and shows how far it is, how long an astronaut would take to walk it, how many Martian days of spacewalk time it needs, and how steep it gets. Behind the scenes, the app sends each pair of consecutive stops to a pathfinding backend, which scores the terrain by slope, surface type, temperature and points of interest. The frontend joins the legs into one route and draws it on the globe.

Benefits: It makes Mars feel like a real place you can navigate instead of a picture in a textbook. Students and curious people can learn where the famous landing sites and volcanoes are and how far apart they are. It also shows the practical side of exploration: the shortest route isn’t always the best one, because slopes, surfaces and temperature all matter.

Intended impact: The goal is to make space science more approachable and to spark interest in planetary exploration, especially for younger users. It can be used in classrooms, at science events or just for fun. The route planner also gives people a taste of the kind of mission planning real teams do when deciding where a rover or astronaut can safely go.

Tools and technologies: The frontend is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript. The 3D globe uses CesiumJS with a Mars terrain tileset streamed from Cesium ion, and the flat map layers use NASA Mars Trek imagery (MOLA color-shaded elevation and the Viking color mosaic). Styling is done with Tailwind CSS. The backend is a separate API that handles the pathfinding. It runs in a normal web browser with WebGL, so no special hardware is needed beyond a regular computer with a graphics-capable browser.

Creativity: Instead of a plain map, the project has a hand-drawn crayon look, an onboarding dialogue, sound effects and a game-style achievement popup when Mars loads, which makes it feel more like a game than a data tool. We wrote our own camera controls so rotation and zoom feel smooth at every height, from the whole planet down to the ground, and the camera can’t clip under the terrain. Turning a pathfinding algorithm into a simple “pick places and go” experience is also part of the creative side.MOLA dataset
